p.src: Sima Yi then memorialized: “I once told Your Majesty that Kongming would surely advance through Chencang, and therefore appointed Hao Zhao to defend it. And now it has happened exactly so. If he were to invade by way of Chencang, transporting provisions would be exceedingly convenient. Fortunately, Hao Zhao and Wang Shuang now hold that place, so he dares not transport provisions by this route, while carriage along the other narrow paths is arduous. By my calculation, the Shu army carries no more than one month’s provisions, so its advantage lies in forcing a swift battle. Our army should simply hold out for a long while. Your Majesty may issue an edict ordering Cao Zhen to defend every pass and strategic point steadfastly and not give battle. Within a month, the Shu troops will withdraw of their own accord. Then we may strike while they are vulnerable. Zhuge Liang can thus be captured.” Cao Rui said delightedly, “Since you possess such foresight, why do you not personally lead an army to attack him?” Sima Yi replied, “It is not that I cherish my person or prize my life. I truly wish to preserve these troops against Lu Xun of Eastern Wu. Before long, Sun Quan will surely usurp the imperial title and proclaim himself sovereign. Once he assumes that dignity, he will fear that Your Majesty intends to punish him and will assuredly invade first. Therefore I wish to keep this army ready for him.”

p.src: While they were speaking, a close attendant suddenly reported, “Commander Cao has submitted a report on the military situation.” Sima Yi said, “Your Majesty should immediately send someone to warn Cao Zhen: whenever he pursues the Shu army, he must first ascertain whether it is strong or weak. He must not penetrate deeply into dangerous ground and fall into Zhuge Liang’s scheme.” Cao Rui immediately issued an edict and dispatched Han Ji, Minister of Ceremonies, bearing the imperial tally, to warn Cao Zhen: “On no account give battle; devote yourself to vigilant defense. Only after the Shu troops have withdrawn may you strike them.” Sima Yi escorted Han Ji beyond the city and charged him: “I yield the credit for this achievement to Zidan. When you see him, do not say that this proposal came from me; say only that the Son of Heaven has issued an edict commanding him to make defense his chief concern. Whoever is sent in pursuit must be chosen with the utmost care; do not send anyone hasty and impetuous.” Han Ji took his leave and departed.

p.src: Meanwhile, Cao Zhen was holding council in his command tent when word suddenly came that the Son of Heaven had dispatched Han Ji, Minister of Ceremonies, bearing the imperial tally. Cao Zhen went out of the camp to receive him and escorted him inside. After receiving the edict, he withdrew and consulted Guo Huai and Sun Li. Guo Huai laughed and said, “This is Sima Zhongda’s counsel.” Cao Zhen asked, “What do you think of this counsel?” Guo Huai replied, “These words show a profound understanding of Zhuge Liang’s methods of warfare. In times to come, the man capable of resisting the Shu army will surely be Zhongda.” Cao Zhen said, “But what if the Shu army does not withdraw?” Guo Huai replied, “We may secretly send someone to instruct Wang Shuang to lead troops in patrolling the narrow paths; then the enemy will not dare transport provisions. When their provisions are exhausted and their troops retreat, we can pursue them with the momentum and win a complete victory.” Sun Li said, “I shall go to Mount Qi and pretend to command a grain convoy. I will fill the wagons entirely with dry firewood and thatch, soak them with sulfur and saltpeter, and then have men spread a false report that provisions have arrived from Longxi. If the Shu troops are short of provisions, they will surely come to seize them. Once they have entered our midst, we shall set the wagons ablaze and support the attack with ambush troops outside. Thus we can defeat them.” Cao Zhen said delightedly, “An excellent plan!” He immediately ordered Sun Li to lead troops and carry out the plan. He also sent a messenger instructing Wang Shuang to patrol the narrow paths with his troops, while Guo Huai was to lead forces in directing the defenses of Jigu and Jieting and order the armies along every route to guard the strategic points. Cao Zhen further appointed Zhang Liao’s son Zhang Hu as vanguard and Yue Jin’s son Yue Chen as deputy vanguard. Together they were to defend the forward camp and were forbidden to give battle.

p.src: Meanwhile, in his camp at Mount Qi, Kongming sent men to challenge the enemy every day, but the Wei troops held firm and would not come out. Kongming summoned Jiang Wei to confer and said, “The Wei troops hold fast and refuse battle because they have reckoned that our army lacks provisions. Transport through Chencang is now blocked, while passage along the other narrow paths is exceedingly difficult. By my calculation, the provisions accompanying the army will not suffice for one month. What are we to do?” As he pondered, a sudden report came that several thousand Wei provision wagons from Longxi were west of Mount Qi, and that the officer commanding the convoy was Sun Li. Kongming asked, “What sort of man is he?” A man of Wei reported, “This man once accompanied the ruler of Wei on a hunt at Mount Dashi. A fierce tiger was suddenly startled from cover and charged straight at the imperial presence; Sun Li dismounted, drew his sword, and slew it. For this he was appointed Senior General. He is one of Cao Zhen’s most trusted men.” Kongming laughed and said, “The Wei generals have reckoned that we lack provisions and therefore devised this scheme. What those wagons carry must be thatch and other kindling. All my life I have made a specialty of fire attacks. Do they now mean to lure me with such a trick? If they learn that our army has gone to seize the provisions, they will surely come to raid our camp. We can turn their own scheme against them.”

p.src: He then summoned Ma Dai and instructed him: “Lead three thousand troops straight to the place where the Wei army has stored its provisions. Do not enter the camp; merely set fires from upwind. Once the wagons and equipment catch fire, the Wei troops will surely come to surround our camp.” He also assigned Ma Zhong and Zhang Ni each to lead five thousand troops and surround the enemy from without, so they could attack from both inside and outside. The three men received the plan and departed. He next summoned Guan Xing and Zhang Bao and instructed them: “The forward camp of the Wei army connects with roads leading in all four directions. If fire rises from the western hills tonight, the Wei troops will surely come to raid our camp. You two are to lie in ambush on either side of the Wei camp. As soon as their troops leave the camp, you may seize it.” He also summoned Wu Ban and Wu Yi and instructed them: “Each of you is to lead one force and lie in ambush outside our camp. When the Wei troops arrive, cut off their route of retreat.” When Kongming had completed his dispositions, he seated himself on the heights of Mount Qi. Wei scouts learned that the Shu troops meant to seize the provisions and hurriedly reported it to Sun Li. Sun Li had a swift report sent to Cao Zhen. Cao Zhen sent a man to the forward camp with these instructions for Zhang Hu and Yue Chen: “Watch for fire rising west of the mountain tonight. The Shu troops will surely come to its aid. You may then send out your troops and proceed thus and thus.” The two men received the plan and ordered men to climb the watchtower and keep their eyes fixed on the fire signal.

p.src: Meanwhile, Sun Li concealed his troops west of the mountain and waited only for the Shu army to arrive. That night, during the second watch, Ma Dai came with three thousand troops; every man held a gag in his mouth, and every horse was bridled to silence it. They went straight west of the mountain, where they saw a great multitude of wagons and equipment, tier upon tier, clustered in a ring to form a camp, with banners stuck here and there among the empty wagons. Just then a southwesterly wind arose. Ma Dai ordered his soldiers to go straight to the south side of the camp and set it ablaze. Every wagon caught fire, and the flames soared to the heavens. Sun Li supposed that the Shu troops had entered the Wei camp and lit the signal fire, so he urgently led all his troops in a sudden rush upon them. Behind him, drums and horns thundered to the sky as troops attacked from two directions: Ma Zhong and Zhang Ni had encircled the Wei army at the very center. Sun Li was greatly alarmed. Then battle cries arose among the Wei ranks, and a fierce body of troops charged out beside the flames: it was Ma Dai. Attacked from within and without, the Wei army suffered a crushing defeat. The flames raged and the wind blew fiercely; men and horses fled in confusion, and the dead were beyond number. Sun Li led the wounded remnants through smoke and fire and escaped.

p.src: Meanwhile, Zhang Hu, seeing the flames soar to the sky from within his camp, threw open the gates and, together with Yue Chen, led out all their troops and charged toward the Shu camp, only to find not a single person there. As they hastily recalled their troops to return, forces under Wu Ban and Wu Yi attacked from two directions and cut off their retreat. Generals Zhang and Yue desperately broke through the encirclement and hurried back to their own camp, only to see arrows flying like locusts from atop its earthen walls. Guan Xing and Zhang Bao had already taken the camp by surprise. The Wei troops were utterly defeated and all fled toward Cao Zhen’s camp. Just as they were about to enter, they saw a battered force racing toward them: it was Sun Li. They entered the camp together, appeared before Cao Zhen, and each related how he had fallen into the enemy’s scheme. When Cao Zhen heard what had happened, he guarded the main camp with the utmost caution and no longer offered battle. The victorious Shu troops returned to report to Kongming.

p.src: Kongming secretly sent a man to deliver a plan to Wei Yan, while ordering all the camps to be struck and the army to depart together. Yang Yi said, “We have now won a great victory and utterly broken the spirit of the Wei army. Why, then, do you mean to withdraw?” Kongming replied, “Our army has no provisions, so our advantage lies in a swift battle. Now that the enemy holds firm and refuses to come out, we are the ones who suffer. Though they have suffered a temporary defeat, reinforcements will surely come from the Central Plains. If their light cavalry strikes our supply route, we shall be unable to return when the time comes. We must take advantage of the Wei army’s recent defeat, while they dare not face the troops of Shu, and withdraw unexpectedly while the opportunity remains. My only concern is Wei Yan’s force, which is holding Wang Shuang at the mouth of the Chencang road and cannot disengage quickly. I have already sent someone with a secret plan instructing him to slay Wang Shuang, so that the men of Wei will not dare pursue us. Let the rear columns depart first.” That night Kongming left only gongs and drums in the camp to sound the watches. By the end of the night the entire army had withdrawn, leaving only an empty camp.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Cao Zhen sat grieving in his camp, a sudden report came that General of the Left Zhang He had arrived with troops. Zhang He dismounted, entered the tent, and said to Cao Zhen, “I have come by imperial command expressly to serve under your direction.” Cao Zhen asked, “Did you speak with Zhongda before you parted?” Zhang He replied, “Zhongda told me: ‘If our army wins, the troops of Shu will not readily depart; but if our army loses, the troops of Shu will surely leave at once.’ Since our defeat, has the Commander-in-Chief sent scouts to learn the movements of the Shu army?” Cao Zhen said, “I have not.” Men were immediately sent to investigate, and indeed the camp was deserted: only several dozen banners stood there, and the army had been gone for two days. Cao Zhen’s regret came too late.

p.src: Now Wei Yan, having received the secret plan, struck camp at the second watch that night and hurried back toward Hanzhong. A spy soon informed Wang Shuang, who drove his troops forward in full force. After pursuing them for more than twenty li, he was nearly upon them. Seeing Wei Yan’s banners ahead, he shouted, “Wei Yan, do not flee!” The troops of Shu did not even look back. Wang Shuang spurred his horse in pursuit. Then the Wei soldiers behind him cried out, “Fire has broken out in the camp outside the city! We fear it is an enemy stratagem.” Wang Shuang hastily reined in and turned. Seeing flames soaring into the sky, he panicked and ordered a retreat. As they reached the left side of a hillside, a lone horseman suddenly burst from the woods and thundered, “Wei Yan is here!” Wang Shuang was so startled that he had no time to defend himself, and Wei Yan cut him down from his horse with one stroke. Believing an ambush lay in wait, the Wei troops scattered and fled. Wei Yan, with only thirty horsemen under his command, rode leisurely toward Hanzhong. A later poet composed verses in praise:

p.src: It turned out that, following Kongming’s ingenious plan, Wei Yan had first left thirty horsemen hidden beside Wang Shuang’s camp; as soon as Wang Shuang led his troops out in pursuit, they were to set fire to his camp; then, when he turned back, Wei Yan was to take him by surprise, charge out, and slay him. Having slain Wang Shuang, Wei Yan led his troops back to Hanzhong, where he presented himself to Kongming and handed over his men and horses. Kongming held a grand celebratory banquet; no more need be said of it.

When Cao Zhen heard this, his grief knew no bounds, and his anguish brought on an illness. He therefore returned to Luoyang, ordering Guo Huai, Sun Li, and Zhang He to guard the various approaches to Chang’an.

p.src: Now Sun Quan, ruler of Wu, was holding court when a spy reported, “Zhuge Liang, Chancellor of Shu, has twice led forth an army, and Cao Zhen, Commander-in-Chief of Wei, has lost troops and generals.” The ministers all urged the King of Wu to raise an army against Wei and seek possession of the Central Plains, but Sun Quan hesitated and could not decide. Zhang Zhao memorialized, “I have lately heard that phoenixes have descended upon East Mountain at Wuchang; and that yellow dragons have repeatedly appeared in the Great River. My lord’s virtue equals that of Yao and Shun, and his wisdom rivals Kings Wen and Wu. You should at once assume the imperial throne and then raise the army.” All the officials agreed, saying, “Zibu speaks truly.” Thus they selected the bingyin day of the fourth month that summer and built a terrace in the southern suburbs of Wuchang. On that day the ministers invited Sun Quan to ascend the terrace and assume the imperial throne, and the eighth year of Huangwu was changed to the first year of Huanglong. He bestowed upon his father, Sun Jian, the posthumous title Emperor Wulie. His mother, Lady Wu, was honored as Empress Wulie. His elder brother, Sun Ce, was honored as Prince Huan of Changsha. He appointed his son Sun Deng as Crown Prince. He named Zhuge Ke, eldest son of Zhuge Jin, Left Mentor to the Crown Prince, and Zhang Xiu, second son of Zhang Zhao, Right Mentor to the Crown Prince.

p.src: Zhuge Ke’s courtesy name was Yuanxun. He stood seven chi tall, was exceptionally clever, and excelled in repartee. Sun Quan was exceedingly fond of him. When Zhuge Ke was six, he attended a banquet in Eastern Wu with his father. Noticing Zhuge Jin’s long face, Sun Quan ordered someone to bring in a donkey and had the words “Zhuge Ziyu” written in chalk upon its face. Everyone burst into laughter. Zhuge Ke hurried forward, took the chalk, and added two characters below, making it read: “Zhuge Ziyu’s donkey.” Everyone present was astonished. Sun Quan was delighted and gave him the donkey. On another day, Sun Quan held a grand banquet for his officials and ordered Zhuge Ke to serve the wine. When he came to Zhang Zhao, Zhang Zhao refused to drink, saying, “This is no way to honor the aged.” Sun Quan said to Zhuge Ke, “Can you make Zibu drink?” Accepting the command, Zhuge Ke said to Zhang Zhao, “In former times Father Shang was ninety years old, yet he bore the yak-tail standard and wielded the battle-axe, and never once spoke of being old. When battle is at hand, sir, you remain in the rear; but when it is time to drink, you stand foremost; how, then, can you say we do not honor the aged?” Zhang Zhao had no answer and was obliged to drink. Sun Quan loved Zhuge Ke for this and therefore appointed him guardian to the Crown Prince. u.src: Zhuge Ke’s courtesy name was Yuanxun. He stood seven chi tall, was exceptionally clever, and excelled in repartee.
Sun Quan was exceedingly fond of him.
When Zhuge Ke was six, he attended a banquet in Eastern Wu with his father.
Noticing Zhuge Jin’s long face, Sun Quan ordered someone to bring in a donkey and had the words “Zhuge Ziyu” written in chalk upon its face.
Everyone burst into laughter.
Zhuge Ke hurried forward, took the chalk, and added two characters below, making it read: “Zhuge Ziyu’s donkey.”
Everyone present was astonished.
Sun Quan was delighted and gave him the donkey.
On another day, Sun Quan held a grand banquet for his officials and ordered Zhuge Ke to serve the wine.
When he came to Zhang Zhao, Zhang Zhao refused to drink, saying, “This is no way to honor the aged.”
Sun Quan said to Zhuge Ke, “Can you make Zibu drink?”

When battle is at hand, sir, you remain in the rear;

p.src: Sun Quan followed his counsel and immediately ordered an envoy to travel day and night into Shu to meet the Later Emperor. After the formal courtesies, the envoy reported the matter in detail. On hearing this, the Later Emperor consulted his ministers. The general opinion was that Sun Quan had usurped an imperial title and that the alliance with him should be severed. Jiang Wan said, “We should send someone to ask the Chancellor.” The Later Emperor immediately dispatched a messenger to Hanzhong to consult Kongming. Kongming said, “Send someone bearing gifts into Wu to offer congratulations, and request that Lu Xun lead an army against Wei. Wei will surely send Sima Yi to resist him. If Sima Yi goes south to oppose Eastern Wu, I shall march out through Qishan once more, and Chang’an may then be taken.” The Later Emperor followed his advice and ordered Grand Commandant Yang Zhen to take fine horses, jade belts, gold, pearls, and other treasures into Wu as congratulatory gifts. When Yang Zhen reached Eastern Wu, he met Sun Quan and presented the state letter. Sun Quan was delighted, entertained him at a banquet, and then sent him back to Shu. Sun Quan summoned Lu Xun and told him of the agreement with Western Shu to raise their armies against Wei. Lu Xun said, “This is Kongming’s scheme, born of his fear of Sima Yi. Since we have agreed to act with him, we cannot refuse. For now, however, let us merely make a show of mobilizing, thereby supporting the troops of Shu from afar. When Kongming presses his attack on Wei, we can exploit the opening and seize the Central Plains.” Orders were issued at once for troops throughout Jingzhou and Xiangyang to be trained and made ready to march on a chosen day.

p.src: Now Chen Zhen returned to Hanzhong and reported everything to Kongming. Kongming was still concerned that Chencang could not be approached lightly, so he first sent scouts to reconnoiter. They returned and reported, “Hao Zhao is gravely ill inside Chencang.” Kongming said, “The great undertaking is as good as accomplished.” He then summoned Wei Yan and Jiang Wei and instructed them, “You two are to take five thousand troops and march through the night straight to the foot of Chencang’s walls; when you see fire break out, join forces and assault the city.” Neither man was fully convinced, and they asked, “On what day are we to set out?” Kongming said, “Have everything ready within three days; there is no need to take leave of me—set out at once.” The two received the plan and departed. He next summoned Guan Xing and Zhang Bao, whispered detailed instructions into their ears, and each departed with a secret plan.

p.src: Meanwhile, when Guo Huai heard that Hao Zhao was gravely ill, he consulted Zhang He, saying, “Hao Zhao is seriously ill. You must hurry there and take his place. I shall write a memorial to the court myself and await its further decision.” Zhang He led three thousand troops and hurried to relieve Hao Zhao. At that time Hao Zhao was near death. While he lay groaning that night, a sudden report came that the Shu troops had reached the city walls. Hao Zhao urgently ordered men onto the walls to defend them. Just then fires broke out at every gate, and the city fell into great disorder. When Hao Zhao heard the news, the shock killed him. The Shu troops surged into the city as one.

p.src: But when Wei Yan and Jiang Wei led their troops to Chencang and looked upon the city, they saw not a single banner, nor did they hear any watchman sounding the night watches. The two were startled and suspicious and dared not attack. Suddenly a cannon boomed, and banners rose on every side. They saw a man in a silk cap, holding a feather fan and wearing a crane-feather cloak over a Daoist robe, cry aloud, “You two have come too late.” They looked and saw that it was Kongming. They hastily dismounted, bowed to the ground, and said, “The Chancellor’s strategy is truly divine!” Kongming had them admitted into the city and said, “I learned through my scouts that Hao Zhao was gravely ill. I ordered you to lead troops and take the city within three days only to reassure everyone. Meanwhile I ordered Guan Xing and Zhang Bao to pretend they were merely mustering troops, then secretly leave Hanzhong. I concealed myself among their troops and marched through the night at double speed straight to the city walls, leaving the enemy no time to move reinforcements. I had already planted agents inside the city to start fires and raise battle cries in support, throwing the Wei troops into fearful confusion. With no commander to lead them, the troops were certain to fall into disorder of their own accord. I seized the city in consequence, as easily as turning over my hand. The Art of War says, ‘Appear where the enemy does not expect you, and attack where he is unprepared.’ This is precisely what it means.” Wei Yan and Jiang Wei bowed to the ground. Kongming pitied Hao Zhao in death and ordered that his wife and children escort his coffin back to Wei, in recognition of his loyalty.

p.src: Kongming said to Wei Yan and Jiang Wei, “Do not remove your armor yet. Lead your troops at once and make a surprise attack on Sanguan Pass. When its defenders learn that your troops have arrived, they are certain to flee in terror. If you delay even a little and Wei troops reach the pass, it will become difficult to take.” Wei Yan and Jiang Wei accepted the order and led their troops straight to Sanguan Pass. Sure enough, all the defenders of the pass fled. The two had just ascended the pass and were about to remove their armor when they saw great clouds of dust rising beyond it: the Wei army was approaching. They said to each other, “The Chancellor’s divine foresight is beyond all fathoming!” They hurried up the tower to look and saw that it was the Wei general Zhang He. The two divided their troops and secured the strategic defiles. Seeing the Shu troops holding the vital routes, Zhang He ordered a retreat. Wei Yan pursued and attacked them for some distance. Countless Wei soldiers were killed, and Zhang He withdrew in crushing defeat. Wei Yan returned to the pass and sent a messenger to report to Kongming. Kongming himself had already led troops out through the Chencang Xie Valley and captured Jianwei. The Shu troops behind him advanced in a steady succession. The Latter Ruler also ordered the general Chen Shi to come to their aid. Kongming drove his great army forth once more to Mount Qi. After establishing camp, Kongming assembled his officers and said, “Twice I have marched from Mount Qi without gaining any advantage. Now that I have come here again, I expect the men of Wei will oppose me on the same battleground as before. They suspect that I intend to take Yong and Mei, and will certainly station troops to defend both places. But I observe that Wudu and Yinping adjoin Han territory. If we obtain those two commanderies, we can also divide the strength of Wei’s forces. Who dares take them?” Jiang Wei said, “I am willing to go.” Wang Ping also said, “I too am willing to go.” Kongming was delighted. He ordered Jiang Wei to lead ten thousand troops to take Wudu and Wang Ping to lead ten thousand to take Yinping. The two received their plans and departed.

p.src: Now Zhang He returned to Chang’an and said to Guo Huai and Sun Li, “Chencang has fallen, Hao Zhao is dead, and Sanguan Pass has also been occupied by the Shu troops. Kongming has now come forth again from Mount Qi and is advancing along several routes.” Guo Huai exclaimed in alarm, “If that is so, he is certain to take Yong and Mei!” He therefore left Zhang He to defend Chang’an and ordered Sun Li to secure Yongcheng. Guo Huai himself led troops through the night to defend Meicheng, while sending a memorial to Luoyang to report the emergency.

p.src: Meanwhile, when the ruler of Wei, Cao Rui, held court, a close attendant reported, “Chencang has fallen, Hao Zhao is dead, Zhuge Liang has again marched from Mount Qi, and Sanguan Pass has also been seized by the Shu troops.” Cao Rui was greatly alarmed. Suddenly it was further reported that Man Chong and the others had submitted a memorial saying, “Sun Quan of Eastern Wu has presumptuously assumed the imperial title and allied himself with Shu. He has now sent Lu Xun to train troops at Wuchang and await orders for deployment. Within a matter of days, he is certain to invade.” Hearing that danger threatened in two quarters, Cao Rui lost his composure and became deeply alarmed. At this time Cao Zhen had not yet recovered from his illness, so Cao Rui summoned Sima Yi to consult with him. Sima Yi said, “In my humble judgment, Eastern Wu will certainly not raise an army.” Cao Rui asked, “How do you know this?” Sima Yi replied, “Kongming has long wished to avenge the defeat at Xiaoting. It is not that he has no desire to swallow Wu, but he fears that the Central Plains would strike him while his lands were undefended, and so he has temporarily allied with Eastern Wu. Lu Xun also understands his intention. Thus he merely makes a show of mobilizing troops in response, while in truth sitting back to watch which side succeeds or fails. Your Majesty need not guard against Wu; you need only guard against Shu.” Cao Rui said, “Yours is truly a discerning judgment!” He then appointed Sima Yi Grand Commander-in-Chief, placing all forces on the various routes through Longxi under his authority, and ordered an attendant to fetch Cao Zhen’s seal of supreme military command. Sima Yi said, “I shall go and fetch it myself.” He took leave of the emperor and departed the court, went straight to Cao Zhen’s residence, and first sent a man inside to announce him before entering to pay his respects.

p.src: After inquiring after his illness, Sima Yi said, “Eastern Wu and Western Shu have joined forces and raised armies to invade us. Kongming has now again marched from Mount Qi and established camp. Are you aware of this, my lord?” Cao Zhen exclaimed in surprise, “My family knew that I was gravely ill and did not let me hear of it. With the state in such peril, why has Zhongda not been appointed commander-in-chief to drive back the Shu army?” Sima Yi said, “My abilities are meager and my wisdom shallow; I am unfit for such an office.” Cao Zhen said, “Bring the seal and give it to Zhongda.” Sima Yi said, “Commander, do not be so hasty. I am willing to lend what strength I have, but I dare not accept this seal.” Cao Zhen sprang up and said, “If you will not assume this responsibility, Zhongda, the realm is in peril! Ill as I am, I shall go before the Son of Heaven and recommend you!” Sima Yi said, “The Son of Heaven has already issued his gracious command; it is only that I dared not accept it.” Cao Zhen was delighted and said, “Now that Zhongda assumes this duty, the Shu army can be driven back.” Seeing Cao Zhen repeatedly yield the seal to him, Sima Yi finally accepted it. He took leave of the ruler of Wei and led his army toward Chang’an to fight a decisive battle with Kongming. Indeed:
